explanations.answer: On the four corners of the land
explanations.explanation: Right on the money, friend. God says, "The end! The end has come upon the four corners of the land." Picture dough pushed all the way out to every corner of the cookie sheet. That's how far this message reaches.

explanations.answer: On the nations around the land
explanations.explanation: I get why you'd look outside the border, but this message is aimed at home. God is speaking "to the land of Israel." He says the end has come upon the four corners of the land, not on the nations around it.

explanations.answer: On the cities of the Philistines
explanations.explanation: The Philistines never come up in this passage, friend. God is talking to the land of Israel here. He says, "The end! The end has come upon the four corners of the land." Those four corners are what He's pointing at.

Ways is the one. God says, "I will judge you according to your ways and repay you for all your abominations." He's judging how they lived, plain and simple. Nobody gets graded on somebody else's batch.
Enemies sounds like a natural pick, but God puts the focus on the people themselves. He says, "I will judge you according to your ways." It's about how they lived, not about who was against them.
Close, because neighbors are always watching how you live. But God doesn't measure them by the folks next door. He says, "I will judge you according to your ways." Their own ways are the measure.

Not this time, friend. God says the opposite: "I will not look on you with pity, nor will I spare you." It's a hard line, and I think it's one of the heavier ones in the passage. He adds that He will punish them for their ways and for the abominations among them.

False is right. God says, "I will not look on you with pity, nor will I spare you, but I will punish you for your ways and for the abominations among you." That's a heavy line, and it's good to just let it be heavy. The pity and the sparing are the part He rules out.
That's the destination. God says, "Then you will know that I am the LORD." Everything in the warning leads to that one thing they will know.
Nope, the idols get no credit here. God says the people will know "that I am the LORD." The knowing points to Him, not to anything they made.
The kings don't get a victory lap in this one. God says, "Then you will know that I am the LORD." What the people come to know is about God, not about their rulers.

Yes, friend. God says, "Disaster! An unprecedented disaster—behold, it is coming!" Unprecedented means it hasn't happened before, and He says it's coming anyway. Nobody can say they've seen this one already.
God says it's coming "very soon," but He never says it passes quickly. He calls it "An unprecedented disaster." That means one like never before.
This one isn't aimed at their enemies. God says it's coming against the land of Israel: "It has roused itself against you." He calls it "An unprecedented disaster," and it's headed their way.
Panic is right. God says, "there is panic on the mountains instead of shouts of joy." That's a swap nobody wants. Joy goes out and panic walks in.
Worship sounds like a mountain thing, but God's picture is a different one. He says there is "panic on the mountains instead of shouts of joy." Worship isn't what He puts on those mountains.
Silence is a quiet guess, but the mountains aren't quiet here. God says there is "panic on the mountains instead of shouts of joy." The shouts of joy are replaced by panic.
That's it. God says, "Then you will know that it is I, the LORD, who strikes the blow." This time He names Himself as the one who strikes. It's the same warning with a longer closing line.
Chance doesn't get any say here. God says, "Then you will know that it is I, the LORD, who strikes the blow." He names who is behind it, and it isn't luck.
The idols aren't sending anything, friend. God says the people will know "that it is I, the LORD, who strikes the blow." He puts His own name on it, not an idol's.
Right on target. God says, "Their violence has grown into a rod to punish their wickedness." The rod grew out of their own violence. Think of dough rising until it fills the whole bowl.
A guiding rod is a nice thought, but this one isn't for guiding. God says the violence grew "into a rod to punish their wickedness." Punishing is its job here.
This rod isn't for defense, friend. God says, "Their violence has grown into a rod to punish their wickedness." The walls aren't part of that picture.
True, and it's a long list. God says, "None of them will remain: none of their multitude, none of their wealth, and nothing of value." Wealth is named right there. Not a crumb of it remains.
It's the other way around. God says, "None of them will remain: none of their multitude, none of their wealth, and nothing of value." Their wealth is on that list. So none of it remains.

Wrath is the word. God says, "Let the buyer not rejoice and the seller not mourn, for wrath is upon the whole multitude." Neither side of the sale gets a reaction, because the wrath covers everybody. It's the whole multitude.
Blessing would make for a happier verse, but that's not what God says. He says, "for wrath is upon the whole multitude." That's why the buyer shouldn't rejoice.

Peace is a gentle pick, but it's not the word here. God says the buyer shouldn't rejoice and the seller shouldn't mourn, "for wrath is upon the whole multitude." Peace shows up later in the passage as something people seek and can't find (Ezekiel 7:25).
Not this time, friend. God says the vision "will not be revoked." That means it can't be taken back. It's a firm line.
False is right. God says, "the vision concerning the whole multitude will not be revoked." Revoked means taken back, and He says this one won't be. There's no undo button on this one.
Not quite, friend. The trumpet blows and everything is ready, "but no one goes to war." God says, "My wrath is upon the whole multitude." The marching never happens.

False is right. God says, "They have blown the trumpet and made everything ready, but no one goes to war, for My wrath is upon the whole multitude." The trumpet's blown and the gear's ready. And still nobody goes out. That's like setting the timer and preheating the oven, then nobody shows up to bake.
Yes, friend. God says, "Those in the country will die by the sword." It's a heavy line, and I think it's right to let it sit that way. The city gets a different mention in the same verse.
The city does get named, but not for the sword. God says those in the city "will be devoured by famine and plague." The sword is for "those in the country."
The temple isn't named in that verse, friend. God says, "Those in the country will die by the sword, and those in the city will be devoured by famine and plague." So the sword goes with the country.
That's it. God says the survivors are "moaning like doves of the valley, each for his own iniquity." Iniquity is the Bible's word for sin. Each one moans over his own.
Harvest is a fair thought, but it's not what the survivors moan over. God says they moan "each for his own iniquity." Iniquity is sin, and that's the word to land on.
Home is a tender guess, but the verse goes another way. God says the survivors moan "each for his own iniquity." Iniquity means sin, and each one carries his own.
True. God says, "Shame will cover all their faces, and all their heads will be shaved." Notice the word all. It's a heavy picture, and I think it's one of the quiet ones in the passage.
God says the opposite. In verse 18 He says, "Shame will cover all their faces." Shame is named, and it covers all their faces.

That's the one. God says their wealth "became the stumbling block that brought their iniquity." Silver and gold couldn't save them, and instead they tripped them up. It's like the shiny new gadget that ends up taking over your whole counter.

explanations.answer: A gift they gave the poor
explanations.explanation: Giving to the poor isn't in this verse, friend. God says their silver and gold "cannot save them," and that it "became the stumbling block that brought their iniquity." So the wealth trips them up.
A wall is protection, but God says their silver and gold "cannot save them in the day of the wrath of the LORD." It's not a wall. It "became the stumbling block that brought their iniquity."

Unclean is right. God says, "Therefore I will make these into something unclean for them." The ornaments became idols, and the idols become something unclean to them. It's the same beautiful ornaments, turned around.
Holy is the opposite direction. God says the ornaments were made into "vile images and detestable idols." Then He says, "I will make these into something unclean for them."
Hidden doesn't show up in the verse, friend. God says, "Therefore I will make these into something unclean for them." Unclean is the word He picks.

Foreigners is right. God says, "I will hand these things over as plunder to foreigners and loot to the wicked of the earth, who will defile them." The very things they made go to outsiders. They don't get to keep them.

The priests aren't the ones receiving it. God says He will hand these things over "as plunder to foreigners and loot to the wicked of the earth." The priests show up later, when instruction from them perishes (Ezekiel 7:26).

The prophets aren't named in that verse, friend. God says He will hand these things over "as plunder to foreigners and loot to the wicked of the earth." A prophet shows up later, when the people seek a vision (Ezekiel 7:26).

That's what God says. "I will bring the most wicked of nations to take possession of their houses." It's a hard line, and I think it's meant to be heard slowly. They take the houses, and the pride of the mighty ends.

The priests aren't the ones taking houses. God says, "I will bring the most wicked of nations to take possession of their houses." Priests come up later in a different line, where instruction from them perishes (Ezekiel 7:26).
God doesn't say neighbors, friend. He says, "I will bring the most wicked of nations to take possession of their houses." It's a nation brought in from outside.
Yes, a prophet. God says, "Then they will seek a vision from a prophet." Right after that comes a hard part: instruction from the priests will perish, and so will counsel from the elders.

The king shows up in the passage, but not as the one they seek a vision from. God says, "Then they will seek a vision from a prophet." The king appears in the last verse, where he will mourn (Ezekiel 7:27).
The soldiers aren't who they go to. God says, "Then they will seek a vision from a prophet." Earlier He says no one goes to war (Ezekiel 7:14).
Not here, friend. God says "instruction from the priests will perish, as will counsel from the elders." So the elders' counsel doesn't last. It's a sign of how hard that time is.
False is right. God says "instruction from the priests will perish, as will counsel from the elders." So there's no counsel left from the elders. That's a lot of voices gone at once.
